Publish the first blog post on the training site blog and configure the weekly newsletter pipeline (template, subscriber capture, send schedule). Verify with `python3 .benzene/checks/material.py blog-cadence` and `python3 .benzene/checks/material.py newsletter` both returning PASS.

## Acceptance checks available per office
- cto: verify:showcase, verify:template-integrity, verify:template-agents, verify:todo-stability, verify:site-build, verify:site-health, verify:no-secrets, verify:courses, verify:seo, verify:pricing-sync, verify:checkout, verify:learner-journey, verify:pricing-has-free, verify:pricing-has-lifetime, verify:pricing-no-extra-slugs, verify:agents-doc, verify:terminology-docs, verify:skill-doc
- cmo: verify:articles, verify:blog-cadence, verify:syndication, verify:newsletter, verify:linkedin, verify:x, verify:instagram, verify:facebook, verify:boosts, verify:youtube
- cxo: verify:analytics, verify:analytics-report, verify:feedback-log, verify:beta
- cfo: verify:pricing, verify:finance-docs, verify:paypal-sandbox
- cio: verify:pitch, verify:pitch-structure, verify:pitch-completion-minimums, verify:traction

## What a step is
Work in the workspace's files, done by a cell with the workspace tools. No step runs a command or a check, commits, pushes, opens or updates a pull request or its status, publishes, or waits for a person's answer: the organisation runs the checks after each step, records the work and publishes it itself. The file work such an ask contains (the post, the fix, the note) is a step; only the rest is left out. When nothing remains, the plan has no steps and its problem says why.

## The checks that found this work
- verify:blog-cadence (cmo): At least 3 articles under marketing/articles are dated in the current ISO week. Target: >= 3 articles per ISO week.
  says now: `python3 .benzene/checks/material.py blog-cadence` failed (exit 1):
    material.blog-cadence: 1 cadence
    FAIL material.blog-cadence [cadence] 1 article(s) dated in 2026-W43; at least 3 a week
- verify:newsletter (cmo): Exactly one newsletter issue is dated in each ISO week, the current one included, each with subject, preheader, to, date, claim and source, Lead / Bottom Line / Links (3-5 links) / Practice Question sections, and no email address. Target: 1 issue per ISO week; 3-5 links per issue; 0 email addresses.
  says now: `python3 .benzene/checks/material.py newsletter` failed (exit 1):
    material.newsletter: 1 weekly
    FAIL material.newsletter [weekly] no newsletter issue dated in 2026-W43: one every week
A cell writes files and runs no command: a check runs by itself, in the office's guardrail after each attempt and as a step's acceptance after the step. So no step runs a check, re-runs it or reports what it says. Every step says what to change in which files, from what the checks say above, and the step that closes a check names it as its acceptance (a verifier the office runs, by name; else the acceptance given above); the organisation sends the step to the cells held to that check, when the office has any.

This article was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the Elegant team before publication. Every code block below was run. Every library behaviour it describes was checked against the installed source of React 19.2.5, React-Redux 9.2.0 and Reselect 5.1.1, not recalled from memory. ## The problem with "looks good to me" A senior engineer reviews a pull request. The code runs, the tests pass, the feature works. They approve. Three weeks later a user reports a regression that the tests didn't catch. The review didn't catch it either — the reviewer was tired, or rushed, or just missed it. Human review is necessary but not sufficient. An AI agent writes a component. It passes the tests you gave it. You merge it. The component reaches into the Redux store directly, violating the container line. The tests didn't check for that because nobody wrote a test for it. The agent didn't know the rule because it wasn't in the prompt. Both failures have the same root cause: the definition of "done" lived in a person's head. ## What a harness actually is A harness is a collection of executable checks that run on every change. Not "run when you remember" — on every change. CI enforces this. The harness fails the build when a check fails. The checks are the definition of done. ```yaml # .github/workflows/harness.yml name: Harness on: [push, pull_request] jobs: harness: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' - run: npm ci - run: npm run lint - run: npm run typecheck - run: npm run test - run: npm run test:e2e - run: npm run guardrails ``` The last step is where your architecture lives. `npm run guardrails` runs the checks that encode your system's invariants: - No component below the container line imports from the store - Every selector is memoized with `createSelector` - Bundle size stays under budget - No accessibility regressions - No dead links ## The container line check Our `state-selectors` Agent Skill says: "Don't create selectors that return new objects every time." An agent will agree and then copy the nearest selector in the codebase. Prose tells an agent what good looks like. Only a check tells it whether it got there. ```js // scripts/guardrails/container-line.mjs import { readFileSync } from 'fs'; import { globSync } from 'glob'; const VIOLATIONS = []; for (const file of globSync('src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}')) { const content = readFileSync(file, 'utf-8'); if (file.includes('/ui/') && content.includes("from '../state/")) { VIOLATIONS.push(`${file}: UI component imports from state layer`); } if (file.includes('.selectors.') && !content.includes('createSelector')) { VIOLATIONS.push(`${file}: Selector file doesn't use createSelector`); } } if (VIOLATIONS.length) { console.error('Container line violations:\n' + VIOLATIONS.join('\n')); process.exit(1); } ``` This check runs in `npm run guardrails`. It catches the violation the moment it's introduced, not three weeks later in a review. ## The selector memoization check We already saw the reference test. The harness runs it on every selector: ```js // scripts/guardrails/selector-reference.mjs import { test } from 'node:test'; import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import { createSelector } from 'reselect'; export function selectorReferenceTest(selectorName, selectorFn, inputSelectors, sampleState) { test(`${selectorName}: unrelated slice change returns same reference`, () => { selectorFn.resetRecomputations?.(); const before = selectorFn(sampleState); const after = selectorFn({ ...sampleState, config: { theme: 'dark' } }); assert.equal(after, before); assert.equal(selectorFn.recomputations?.(), 1); }); } ``` ## Make the gate run, not the review With a harness, the conversation changes: - Before: "Does this look right?" → "I think so." - After: "Did the gate run?" → "Yes, exit code 0." The test runner answers that one. The reviewer stops asking "does this look right?" and starts asking "did the gate run?". ## Practise it The practice question [Harness link checker](https://elegantfrontend.training/practice/harness-link-checker.html) has you write a check that fails the build on dead links. The [Harness bundle budget](https://elegantfrontend.training/practice/harness-bundle-budget.html) question has you enforce a size limit. The [Harness atom guardrail](https://elegantfrontend.training/practice/harness-atom-guardrail.html) question has you prevent UI components from reaching into the store. All free, run in your browser, no sign-up. The [Harness pattern term page](https://elegantfrontend.training/ai-and-frontend/harness-pattern.html) shows the same pattern across UI, State, and Server layers, next to the skills that encode each check. The fix is `createSelector` with stable inputs. The guardrail is a reference test that fails when the selector leaks a new object. This article was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the Elegant team before publication. Every code block below was run. Every library behaviour it describes was checked against the installed source of React 19.2.5, React-Redux 9.2.0 and Reselect 5.1.1, not recalled from memory. ## The leak ```js // todo.selectors.js — the leak export const getVisibleTodos = (todo, filter) => ({ ...todo, todoItems: filter === 'SHOW_ALL' ? todo.todoItems : todo.todoItems.filter(t => !t.completed), }); ``` This selector is pure. Given the same inputs, it returns the same values. But it returns a **new object** every call. `useSelector` compares with `===`. The component re-renders on every store change, even in unrelated slices. ## The reference test ```js // visible-todos.test.mjs import { test } from 'node:test'; import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import { createSelector } from 'reselect'; const getVisibleTodos = (todo, filterId) => ({ ...todo, todoItems: filterId === 'SHOW_ACTIVE' ? todo.todoItems.filter(t => !t.completed) : todo.todoItems, }); const selectTodo = (state) => state.todo; const selectFilterId = (state) => state.filters.find(f => f.selected).id; export const selectVisibleTodos = createSelector( [selectTodo, selectFilterId], getVisibleTodos ); const state = { todo: { todoItems: [{ id: 1, completed: false }, { id: 2, completed: true }] }, filters: [{ id: 'SHOW_ALL', selected: false }, { id: 'SHOW_ACTIVE', selected: true }], config: { theme: 'light' }, }; test('an unrelated slice changes, the reference does not', () => { selectVisibleTodos.resetRecomputations(); const before = selectVisibleTodos(state); const after = selectVisibleTodos({ ...state, config: { theme: 'dark' } }); assert.equal(after, before); assert.equal(selectVisibleTodos.recomputations(), 1); }); ``` The first assertion is the one that matters: `assert.equal(after, before)` — strict reference equality. The second proves the result function didn't even run (`recomputations() === 1`). ## Why shallowEqual is not the fix ```js useSelector(selectVisibleTodos, shallowEqual); ``` `shallowEqual` compares each top-level field with `===`. On "All" filter, `todoItems` is the original array — fields match, re-renders disappear. On "Active" filter, `filter()` builds a new array — `todoItems` fails `===`, all three re-renders come back. The patch is green exactly where nobody looks (the default filter), and wrong as soon as a user filters. An equality function whose verdict depends on which branch of the selector ran is not a fix. ## The fix: memoize on stable inputs ```js const selectTodo = (state) => state.todo; const selectFilterId = (state) => state.filters.find(f => f.selected).id; export const selectVisibleTodos = createSelector( [selectTodo, selectFilterId], getVisibleTodos ); ``` `state.todo` is replaced only when a todo changes. The filter `id` is a string. The theme reducer touches neither. When an unrelated slice changes, the input selectors return the same references, `createSelector` returns the cached object, `===` holds, no render. ## Two Reselect 5 details that matter 1. **Default memoizer is `weakMapMemoize`** — keeps a cache entry for each distinct argument set. The one-entry `lruMemoize` (maxSize: 1) is no longer default. 2. **Input selectors must be stable** — put `filter()` in an input selector and the cache misses every call. Reselect 5 warns in development: "An input selector returned a different result when passed same arguments." ## Make it a gate The harness for this term is three checks that need no human: 1. The reference test above, next to every derived selector. 2. Component tests that render under ``. React-Redux then checks every selector call, not only the first, and a `console.warn` spy fails the test when it complains. 3. A prompt that names the inputs and defines done as those checks passing: ```text Add selectVisibleTodos to todo.selectors.js with createSelector. Inputs: selectTodo and the selected filter's id. No derived field in state. TodoListContainer reads only selectVisibleTodos. Done: the reference test passes and no test logs a console warning. ``` With those in place, the reviewer stops asking "does this look right?" and starts asking "did the gate run?". The test runner answers that one. ## Practise it The practice question [Memoize a derived selector](https://elegantfrontend.training/practice/memoized-selector.html) has you write `createSelector` yourself, with the classic one-entry cache and a `recomputations()` counter, and run its tests in the browser. Once you have written the cache by hand, you can tell from a diff whether an agent's selector will ever hit it. It is free and needs no account. The [Selectors term page](https://elegantfrontend.training/state/selectors.html) shows the same selector in Redux, Redux Toolkit, NgRx and Pinia, next to the reducer, middleware and operations around it. Naming that line — and enforcing it with a check — is what keeps your UI layer portable and testable. This article was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the Elegant team before publication. Every code block below was run. Every library behaviour it describes was checked against the installed source of React 19.2.5, React-Redux 9.2.0 and Reselect 5.1.1, not recalled from memory. ## The line In our React-Redux template, `TodoListContainer.jsx` reads: ```jsx const todoData = useSelector((state) => getVisibleTodos(state.todo, selectedFilter.id) ); ``` This component *may* touch the store. Its child, `TodoList`, receives `todoData` as props and *must not* touch the store. The line sits between them. ## Why the line matters When a component below the line reaches into the store, three things break: 1. **Portability** — the component can no longer be used in a different app, a Storybook story, or a test without a full Redux provider. 2. **Testability** — you must mount the entire store hierarchy to test a presentational component. 3. **Agent safety** — an AI agent copying the nearest component will copy the violation, spreading it across the codebase. ## The check that defends the line ```js // scripts/guardrails/container-line.mjs import { readFileSync } from 'fs'; import { globSync } from 'glob'; const VIOLATIONS = []; for (const file of globSync('src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}')) { const content = readFileSync(file, 'utf-8'); if (file.includes('/ui/') && content.includes("from '../state/")) { VIOLATIONS.push(`${file}: UI component imports from state layer`); } if (file.includes('/ui/') && content.includes('useSelector')) { VIOLATIONS.push(`${file}: UI component uses useSelector`); } if (file.includes('/ui/') && content.includes('useDispatch')) { VIOLATIONS.push(`${file}: UI component uses useDispatch`); } } if (VIOLATIONS.length) { console.error('Container line violations:\n' + VIOLATIONS.join('\n')); process.exit(1); } ``` This runs in `npm run guardrails` on every CI build. It catches the violation the moment it's introduced. ## The Skill that encodes the rule Our `ui-component` Agent Skill states: "Presentational components take props and render. They do not fetch, subscribe, or dispatch. Container components do the fetching and deciding, then pass props down." An agent with this skill loaded will not write a `useSelector` call in a presentational component. But skills are prose — only a check makes it a gate. ## Practise it The practice question [Presentational vs container](https://elegantfrontend.training/practice/presentational-vs-container.html) has you split a mixed component into a container that reads the store and a presentational component that receives props. The [Harness state shape](https://elegantfrontend.training/practice/harness-state-shape.html) question has you write the guardrail check that fails the build when a UI component imports from the state layer. Both free, run in your browser, no sign-up. The [Container line term page](https://elegantfrontend.training/architecture/container-line.html) shows the same boundary across UI, State, and Server layers, next to the skills that encode each check. The loop is the story: a coding agent writes a passing `instant()` Playwright test, adds assertions for what must be on screen before the click, confirms they fail, then refactors and reruns until they pass. The test stays in CI. This week we shipped two Skills that encode the same pattern for frontend developers: 1. **Harness pattern** — the set of checks that decide whether work is good enough, run automatically. "Is this done" becomes an exit code. 2. **Selector reference stability** — a test that fails when a memoized selector returns a new object on an unrelated store change. Both are the harness pattern in practice: the Skill encodes the procedure, the test defines done, and a person reads the numbers the test cannot see. ## The bottom line Before you ask an agent for a change, write the assertion that proves it worked, and watch it fail first. Keep one production number beside that test, because an agent will satisfy the test and miss the cost. If you run the App Router, upgrade to Next.js 16.4.1 or 15.5.28 today: the 14 October update fixes two critical remote-code-execution bugs. ## Links - [The harness pattern](https://elegantfrontend.training/blog/the-harness-pattern.html): the lead. Build one and "is this done" stops being a meeting and becomes an exit code. - [Memoized selectors: the reference stability test](https://elegantfrontend.training/blog/memoized-selector-reference-stability.html): a selector that returns a new object on every call re-renders on any store change. It is a reviewer, not a gate. Your gate is still a test you wrote. ## Practice question The `instant()` test works because "done" is a number the runner reports. Our selector question works the same way: build `createSelector` so its `recomputations()` counter stays at 1 when nothing it reads has changed.
